topics.name: Cells and Specialised Cells
facts: Cells are tiny structures found in all living things and contain specialised parts called organelles.
Animal and plant cells both contain a nucleus, cytoplasm and a cell membrane.
Plant cells also contain a cell wall, a vacuole and chloroplasts.
The nucleus contains DNA, which carries genetic information and controls the cell's activities.
The cytoplasm is a jelly-like substance where most chemical reactions happen.
The cell membrane controls which substances can enter and leave the cell.
The mitochondria is where energy is released during respiration.
The cell wall provides strength and support to plant cells.
The vacuole contains cell sap.
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll for photosynthesis.
Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts of plant cells.
Specialised cells are adapted for a specific function; structure (shape) relates to function (job).
A sperm cell has a tail to help it swim for reproduction.
A neurone (nerve cell) is adapted to carry electrical signals in the nervous system.
A root hair cell is a specialised plant cell that absorbs water and minerals from the soil.

retrieval_questions.q: What is the function of the nucleus?
retrieval_questions.a: It contains DNA which carries genetic information and controls the cell's activities.

retrieval_questions.a: A jelly-like substance where most chemical reactions happen.

retrieval_questions.q: What is contained in the vacuole?

retrieval_questions.a: To carry electrical signals in the nervous system.

retrieval_questions.a: It is adapted for a specific function.

topics.name: Ecosystems, Food Webs and Sampling
facts: A food chain is a series of organisms living in the same ecosystem, e.g. Grass to Grasshopper to Frog to Hawk.
Food chains always begin with a producer, an organism that can photosynthesise to produce its own glucose.
Primary consumers eat producers and are often herbivores (only eat plants).
Secondary and tertiary consumers may be herbivores or omnivores.
An apex predator sits at the top of the food chain.
Arrows in a food chain show the direction in which energy moves from one organism (trophic level) to the next.
A food web is a collection of interconnected food chains.
Bioaccumulation: toxins pass up the food chain and high levels can end up in organisms at the top.
Sampling lets scientists count organisms in a small area and scale up to the total area.
A sweep net catches insects by sweeping through long grass or vegetation.
A pooter collects small insects by gently sucking them into a container without harming them.
A pitfall trap is a container buried in the ground to catch small insects walking on the surface.
Quadrat sampling uses a square frame to count plants or slow-moving organisms.
To estimate a population: count organisms in several quadrats, calculate the mean per quadrat, then multiply by the total number of quadrats that fit in the area.
Example: 25 dandelions in 5 quadrats = mean of 5 per quadrat; if 100 quadrats fit the field, estimated total = 5 x 100 = 500.

retrieval_questions.q: What is a food chain?
retrieval_questions.a: A series of organisms in an ecosystem showing how energy passes from one to the next.

retrieval_questions.q: What is a food web?
retrieval_questions.a: A collection of interconnected food chains.

retrieval_questions.q: What is interdependence?
retrieval_questions.a: When organisms rely on each other in their food chain/ecosystem for survival.

retrieval_questions.q: What is bioaccumulation?
retrieval_questions.a: The build-up of toxins as they pass up the food chain, ending up in high levels in top organisms.

retrieval_questions.q: What is a producer?
retrieval_questions.a: An organism that can photosynthesise to make its own glucose.

retrieval_questions.q: What is a primary consumer?
retrieval_questions.a: An organism that eats producers, often a herbivore.

retrieval_questions.q: What is a secondary consumer?
retrieval_questions.a: An organism that eats primary consumers.

retrieval_questions.q: What is an apex predator?
retrieval_questions.a: The animal at the top of the food chain.

retrieval_questions.q: What do arrows in a food chain represent?
retrieval_questions.a: The direction in which energy moves between organisms.

retrieval_questions.a: Because counting every organism in a large area would be impractical; sampling gives an accurate estimate.

topics.name: Particles and States of Matter
facts: Matter exists in three states: solid, liquid and gas.
Particles in a solid have little energy, vibrate on the spot, are tightly packed and arranged in neat rows.
Particles in a liquid are close together but move around one another, allowing the liquid to flow; no fixed arrangement.
Particles in a gas have lots of energy, are far apart and move freely and randomly.
Heating supplies energy so particles move more and can overcome the forces of attraction between them, causing a change of state.
Melting point: the temperature at which a substance changes from solid to liquid.
Boiling point: the temperature at which a substance changes from liquid to gas.
Freezing is liquid to solid (occurs at the melting point).
Condensing is gas to liquid (occurs at the boiling point).
Pure substances have fixed melting and boiling points, which can be used to identify them.
Pure water has a melting point of 0°C and a boiling point of 100°C.
Impurities (e.g. salt) lower the melting point and raise the boiling point of water.

retrieval_questions.q: What are the three states of matter?
How are particles arranged in a solid?
retrieval_questions.a: Tightly packed in neat rows, vibrating on the spot.

retrieval_questions.q: How are particles arranged in a liquid?
retrieval_questions.a: Close together but able to move around one another, no fixed arrangement.

retrieval_questions.q: How are particles arranged in a gas?
retrieval_questions.a: Far apart, moving freely and randomly with lots of energy.

retrieval_questions.a: It raises the boiling point above 100°C.

topics.name: Periodic Table: Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
facts: Elements are chemically pure - made of only one type of atom.
Compounds are made of more than one type of atom chemically bonded together.
Mixtures contain different types of atom in the same place but are not chemically bonded.
Mixtures are easier to separate into their components than compounds.
Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is a compound because it contains two different elements (carbon and oxygen) chemically bonded.
A molecule of carbon dioxide is made of one carbon atom bonded to two oxygen atoms.
Compounds can only be separated by chemical reactions, not physical methods.
Mixtures can be separated by physical methods such as filtering, distillation or evaporation.

retrieval_questions.a: Because it contains two different types of atom (carbon and oxygen) chemically bonded together.

topics.name: Forces
facts: Forces can be described as a push, pull or twist.
Contact forces require objects to be touching; non-contact forces act at a distance.
Friction is a contact force that opposes motion when an object moves and particles get in the way.
The three friction forces are friction, drag and air resistance.
Forces always act in opposite pairs - there is always a reaction force.
Balanced forces are equal in size and opposite in direction; the object's motion does not change.
Unbalanced forces change an object's motion - its direction, speed or shape.
Free body (force) diagrams use arrows to show the size and direction of forces.
The resultant force is the overall force acting on an object, calculated by subtracting opposing forces.
The resultant force acts in the direction of the larger force.
Example: 30 N to the left and 10 N to the right gives a resultant of 20 N to the left.
Independent variable: what is changed in an experiment.
Dependent variable: what is measured to get results.
Control variables: factors kept the same to ensure a valid test.
In the spring extension experiment: independent variable = force applied; dependent variable = extension of spring; controls = same spring, same starting point, same measuring method.

retrieval_questions.q: What type of force requires objects to touch?
What type of force acts at a distance?
What force opposes motion between surfaces?

What happens to an object when forces on it are unbalanced?
retrieval_questions.a: Its motion changes - direction, speed or shape.

retrieval_questions.q: What is the independent variable?
retrieval_questions.a: The variable that is changed in the experiment.

retrieval_questions.q: What is the dependent variable?
retrieval_questions.a: The variable that is measured to get results.

retrieval_questions.q: What is a control variable?
retrieval_questions.a: A variable that must be kept the same to ensure a valid test.

retrieval_questions.q: In the spring extension experiment, what is the independent variable?
retrieval_questions.a: The force applied to the spring.

retrieval_questions.q: In the spring extension experiment, what is the dependent variable?
In a parachute experiment varying parachute size, what is the dependent variable?
retrieval_questions.a: The time taken for the object to fall.

topics.name: Space
facts: The Sun is a star at the centre of our solar system, made mostly of hot gases.
The Sun produces light and heat through nuclear reactions.
The Sun's gravity keeps the planets in orbit around it.
A galaxy is a huge collection of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity.
Our solar system is in the Milky Way galaxy, which contains billions of stars.
The planets in order from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune ('My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming').
Inner rocky planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars.
Outer planets (gas/ice giants): Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system.
The further a planet is from the Sun, the longer it takes to complete one orbit.
A moon is a natural object that orbits a planet (Jupiter has many moons).
Gravity is a force that pulls objects towards each other; on Earth it pulls objects towards the ground.
Mass is the amount of matter in an object and does not change anywhere in the universe.
Weight is the force of gravity acting on a mass and depends on the gravitational field strength.
Equation: weight = mass × gravitational field strength (W = m × g).
Gravity on Earth = 9.8 N/kg; gravity on the Moon = 1.6 N/kg.
A satellite is anything that orbits a planet; natural satellites (e.g. the Moon) occur naturally; artificial satellites are man-made for communication, weather monitoring and navigation.
Satellites stay in orbit because gravity pulls them towards Earth while their forward motion keeps them moving around it.

retrieval_questions.q: What is the Sun?
retrieval_questions.a: A star at the centre of our solar system.

retrieval_questions.a: Weight = mass × gravitational field strength (W = m × g).

retrieval_questions.q: What is a natural satellite?
retrieval_questions.a: An object such as the Moon that orbits a planet naturally.

retrieval_questions.q: What is an artificial satellite?
retrieval_questions.a: A man-made object placed in orbit (e.g. for communication, weather or navigation).

retrieval_questions.q: What galaxy is our solar system in?

retrieval_questions.q: What is a galaxy?
retrieval_questions.a: A huge collection of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity.

retrieval_questions.q: Why do satellites stay in orbit?
retrieval_questions.a: Gravity pulls them towards Earth while their forward motion keeps them moving around it.
